body.text: Professor Asad Ghanem is a political scientist at the University of Haifa in Israel and a prominent scholar of Palestinian politics, ethnic states, and minority representation.

His work has examined the political status of Palestinian citizens of Israel, Palestinian governance, and the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. He is the author of several books, including Palestinian Politics after Arafat: A Failed National Movement and The Palestinian-Arab Minority in Israel, 1948–2000.

Speaking over the phone from Haifa, Ghanem discussed the place of Palestinian citizens within Israel’s political system, the ideological differences among Arab parties, and the consequences of Israel’s rightward political shift. He also spoke about the impact of the Gaza war, and why polling turnout among Palestinian voters remains significantly below that of Jewish Israelis.
How is the political and constitutional position of Palestinian citizens of Israel different from that of Palestinians living in the occupied West Bank, East Jerusalem and Gaza?

This goes back to the founding moment in 1948, during the Nakba, when the majority of Palestinians were expelled and became refugees. Around 1,50,000 Palestinians remained. Palestinians who remained within Israel eventually received Israeli citizenship, while other Palestinians were in the West Bank, Gaza, or refugee camps.

The main difference is that Palestinians in Israel hold Israeli citizenship. They have basic political rights. Although Israel has never treated them as fully equal citizens, they have the right to vote, to stand for election, and to be represented in the Knesset.

There is another side to this. The Palestinian national movement developed largely in the refugee camps and later in the West Bank and Gaza. Palestinian citizens of Israel are Palestinians, but historically they have also been somewhat outside the main institutions of the Palestinian national movement.

At the same time, they participate in Israeli politics according to the rules of the Israeli political system. They establish registered political parties, contest elections, and try to use their citizenship and representation to influence decision-making.
When the media refer to “Arab parties” or an “Arab list” in Israel, what exactly does that mean? What are the main ideological currents?

The situation has changed considerably over time. In the 1950s, there was the Communist Party, which represented opposition to government policies, and there were also Arab lists affiliated with Mapai, the dominant Israeli governing party of that period.
From the 1970s, and particularly from the 1980s onwards, the political landscape became much more diverse.

Today, there is a communist current, which is a joint Jewish-Arab political movement. There is also a Palestinian nationalist current and an Islamic current. The Islamic Movement itself has two branches, one participating in parliamentary politics and another remaining outside parliament. Some Palestinian citizens vote for, and are active within, predominantly Jewish parties.

So, when we speak about Arab politics in Israel, we are not talking about one ideological bloc. There are communist, Palestinian nationalist, and Islamist currents, alongside Arabs who participate in Jewish political parties.

Ra’am, the United Arab List led by Mansour Abbas, joined the governing coalition in 2021. Did that experiment show that Palestinian citizens can gain more by participating in government, or did it reveal the limits of seeking equality within a state that defines itself as Jewish?

There is a major debate among Palestinian citizens of Israel over precisely this question. The nationalist parties and the Communist Party have generally refused to participate in Israeli governments. They do not want to assume responsibility for Israeli government policies, particularly policies towards Gaza and the West Bank, as well as broader foreign and domestic policies.

Ra’am took a different position. In 2021, it made it clear that it was willing to participate in government and become part of the balance of power between the political blocs. Its approach is much more focussed on civic issues. It talks about equality, education, allocation of budgets, land, and other resources. The other Arab parties place greater emphasis on ideological and national questions, including resolving the Israeli-Palestinian conflict and Palestinian statehood.
This is the central difference. Ra’am is prepared to enter a coalition and participate directly in decision-making, while the other parties have placed much greater conditions on such participation.
Arab parties and candidates have repeatedly faced attempts to disqualify them in Israeli elections. What is happening in the present election?

Israeli law provides a mechanism through which parties or candidates can be challenged and prevented from contesting elections. Over roughly the past 30 years, almost every election has seen attempts to disqualify at least one Arab party or candidate.

What is particularly significant this time is the breadth of the challenges. Arab parties representing different political tendencies, whether Islamist, nationalist or communist, have faced attempts at disqualification.

These decisions then go before the Supreme Court. We are now waiting for final decisions in several cases involving Arab parties and candidates. [Israel’s Supreme Court has overturned the Central Elections Committee’s decision to bar the Arab-majority Joint List from running in the upcoming election. The court also struck down a ban on the Arab Islamist party Ra’am.]
How have the Gaza war since October 2023, the debate over Palestinian statehood, and developments in the occupied West Bank affected Palestinian citizens of Israel?

This has been a historic turning point. Israeli society has moved further to the right and has become much more militant towards Palestinians. In my view, what has happened in Gaza amounts to genocide, while we are also seeing ethnic cleansing in parts of the West Bank. Palestinian citizens of Israel have been deeply affected.
Relations between the state and the Palestinian minority have deteriorated dramatically. Palestinian citizens have come under growing pressure from the government and state institutions.

October 7 has become a defining political moment inside Israel. The atmosphere now suggests that Palestinians are not permitted the same space for political expression that existed before October 7. In many ways, the war in Gaza has placed Palestinian citizens of Israel in danger. Their citizenship status is, at least partially, being eroded.
We were never equal before October 7, but today we face a much greater danger. There is considerable support within Israeli society for restricting the citizenship rights of Palestinians in Israel.

Much of the opposition is also reluctant to accept even Mansour Abbas, who wants to participate in a governing coalition, because he is an Arab. His participation challenges what I would describe as Jewish political hegemony. This is a major challenge for Palestinian citizens of Israel.
Palestinian citizens constitute a substantial share of Israel’s population, but their presence in the Knesset is proportionately smaller. Why?

There is partly a demographic explanation. Palestinian citizens have a younger population, so a larger proportion are under 18 and cannot vote. Among eligible voters, Arabs constitute around 16 per cent.

But that does not fully explain the gap in parliamentary representation. The larger problem is mistrust. Many Palestinian citizens do not trust the Israeli state and its policies. At the same time, many also do not trust their own political leadership. As a result, many do not vote. Turnout among Arab voters has been around 50 per cent in recent elections, compared with roughly 75 per cent among Jewish voters.
From my point of view, this is a serious mistake. Palestinian citizens need to participate as fully as possible in elections to maximise their representation.

There is also frustration over divisions among the Arab parties. Many Palestinian citizens would prefer the parties to contest elections together on a single list, but the political leadership has repeatedly failed to maintain such unity.

I expect the turnout among Arab voters to rise this time because of Israeli government policies and the wider political atmosphere. It could reach around 60 per cent. That would be significant, but it would still not be enough to fully reflect the community’s potential political weight.

Where, then, does the future of Palestinian political participation lie? Is it in deeper integration into Israeli parliamentary and coalition politics, in building an independent political bloc, or in demanding a more fundamental transformation of the Israeli state?

The situation today is very different from that of the 1990s. At that time, there was a greater balance between the Israeli right and left, and Arab parties could play a crucial role. That gave Palestinian citizens greater political influence.

Today, the entire Israeli political map has shifted to the right. The question for Palestinian citizens is therefore no longer simply whether to cooperate with the right or the left. Much of the political spectrum has moved in a direction that is deeply problematic for Arabs.

At the same time, Palestinian citizens care greatly about their civic status. They want to preserve their citizenship rights, and they are not going to give them up. If Arab political parties become more effective, participation could rise substantially, perhaps to 70 or even 80 per cent. That would increase their political weight.

But there is also a deeper issue. In the long term, many Palestinian citizens seek a transformation in the character of the state because, in their view, defining Israel exclusively as a Jewish state prevents Arabs from achieving full equality.

Palestinian citizens have no real alternative but to continue demanding equal rights in their homeland and a more democratic political order, what we describe as a “state of all its citizens.” I am not optimistic. But I do not see another path open to Palestinian citizens of Israel.

Whether change becomes possible will depend not only on Arab politics inside Israel. It will also depend on wider Palestinian politics, developments in the Arab world, and the degree of international pressure on Israel.
If greater pressure produces a different political balance inside Israel, there may be space for the country to move away from increasingly aggressive, anti-democratic and racist politics.
Iftikhar Gilani is an Indian journalist based in Ankara.
